liveLessons 001 · 037 · 053measured on your device + models

Zombie Horde Lab

Drag from 500 to 8,000 zombies and watch "check everyone" collapse the frame rate. Then switch on the spatial grid. Lesson 037 moves the horde to a 2 km city: choose a grid, a coarse grid, a quadtree or a BVH for each question. Lesson 053 gives the 5,000 zombies brains: spread their thinking over frames and let far zombies think less.

  • O(n²): ×4 work per doubling
  • Frame budget of 16.67 ms
  • A real scaling test on your phone
  • One structure per question: grid, quadtree, BVH
  • Clumped vs spread crowds
  • 053: time slicing and AI LOD
Open lab →

Frame Pipeline Lab

Replay the night-city story: a week of CPU work that changed nothing, the resolution test, and the fixes that reach 60 fps. Then see what the screen really shows (a "60 fps" counter with repeated frames, tearing and uneven camera steps) and why new players hitch the first time a new lake appears.

  • CPU-bound or GPU-bound?
  • Wait markers in the profiler
  • The VSync trap
  • Lesson 059: frame pacing, delta time and VRR
  • Lesson 060: shader compile stutter and PSO lists

Profiler Detective Lab

The FPS counter says 65, players say it's choppy. Find the one bad frame in 300, read its capture, and prove the fix. Then the Reef's net hitch: three written hypotheses, each with a number, and the one test that tells them apart.

  • Average vs P99 vs worst frame
  • Total time, self time and calls
  • Editor vs target build
  • Hypotheses that predict a number
  • Tests where the guesses disagree

liveLessons 004–006 · 010measured on your device

Cache Lab

A real 500,000-particle pool. Lesson 004: after 3 seconds of play the update gets several times slower; fix it with swap-and-pop. Lesson 005: 64-byte particles waste most of every cache line; split them into arrays and watch the bytes drop from 128 MB to 22 MB. Lesson 006: mix rain and blood at random and watch half the CPU's guesses go wrong; fix it with branchless code, SIMD, and splitting by kind.

  • Cache lines and next-door reads
  • Free list vs swap-and-pop
  • AoS vs SoA: loaded vs used bytes
  • Branch guesses, branchless code and SIMD lanes
  • Lesson 010 challenge: predict, then check
  • Lesson 040: allocation-free gameplay code (Reel-in)
  • Lesson 041: pooling done right (fireworks finale)
  • Lesson 042: hidden costs (market board)
Open lab →

Memory & GC Lab

The big fight makes 64 KB of garbage per frame. Watch the heap's free room fill and the game stop for 18 ms every 3.7 seconds. Then remove the garbage with a pool, an arena and cached HUD strings, or hide it with incremental GC.

  • How often vs how long: garbage rate vs live data
  • GC.Collect and the GC Alloc column
  • Pools, frame arenas and incremental GC
  • Lesson 010 challenge: predict, then check
Open lab →
liveLessons 008–010simulation

Jobs Lab

Lesson 008: the storm's 2,000,000 particles on 1 to 8 threads. Eight threads give only 2×: watch each thread's timeline fill with lock waiting and false sharing, then fix both and hit Amdahl's limit. Lesson 009: the whole frame as jobs. Complete() at once keeps 8 cores 19% busy; a task graph with batches takes the frame from 13.41 to 5.64 ms.

  • Threads vs cores and Amdahl's law
  • Lock contention vs per-thread lists
  • False sharing: 8 counters, one cache line
  • Jobs, dependencies and the critical path
  • How big a job should be
  • Lesson 010 challenge: predict, then check
Open lab →

Game Loop Lab

One jump on a 30 fps phone, a 60 Hz PC and a 144 Hz PC. With a variable step the jump peaks at 1.500, 1.583 and 1.632 m, and an autosave hitch drops the player through the floor. Switch to a fixed step with an accumulator, then fix the judder and the spiral of death.

  • Variable vs fixed timestep
  • Tunneling: one 0.25 s step skips the floor
  • The accumulator and interpolation
  • Spiral of death and the step cap

ECS Lab

The Reef: 10,000 fish, birds, crabs and gulls on a 30 fps phone. Store them as a fat base class (1.90 ms per step), as components (2.75 ms) or in ECS (0.11 ms), and watch how the CPU walks through memory. Lesson 013: a storm of status effects costs 1.31 ms on archetype tables, 0.54 ms on sparse sets and 0.21 ms on a hybrid.

  • Class tree vs components vs ECS
  • Fat base class: 320 bytes per critter
  • Packed columns and systems
  • Structural changes: tag vs field
  • Archetype tables vs sparse sets vs hybrid
  • Lesson 022 challenge: Whale Week, predict then check

Events Lab

The Feeding Frenzy: 600 catches per step, and five systems want to know about each one. Tell them with direct calls (15 wires), an event bus (1.03 ms and a GC every 0.9 s), a typed bus or an event queue (0.33 ms, 0 B), and catch the bugs each one brings.

  • Coupling: wires vs links
  • Boxing, list copies and garbage
  • Cascades and re-entrancy
  • Cold vs warm reaction work
  • Queues: delay, order and claiming

Sky Hopper's 1,840 scripts in 10 modules on 6 layers. Pick a module to edit and see what recompiles: 48 s in one assembly, still 48 s when 4 bad arrows tie 8 modules into a tangle. Cut the arrows and a HUD edit drops to 12 s; add an allow-list and the replay server runs with no GPU.

Tuning Lab

Mia tunes the Feeding Frenzy. Apply a change with numbers in code (899 s), in data files (100 s) or with live reload (15 s), and watch 120 tweaks drop from 30 hours to 30 minutes. Break the data with a typo, turn on the validator, then bake it so the phone loads it in 40 ms instead of 1,900. Then move the gulls' steal rule into a hot-reloaded script: 10 hours of tries become 10 minutes, until reloads reset the hunger and old rules keep running.

  • Code says how, data says how much
  • Live tuning between ticks; read, don't copy
  • Schemas, validators and stable IDs
  • Source data vs baked runtime data
  • String lookups vs typed structs
  • Scripting layers, hot reload and its traps
  • Guarded script calls; batching across the boundary

  • Seams and extension points (sockets)
  • Manifests and discovery: scan vs baked list

GPU Pipeline Lab

The Reef's Coral Garden needs 41 ms of GPU time on a mid-range phone. Halve the coral triangles and gain 0 ms. Then pull one lever at a time (triangles, render scale, a flat test shader, a 4-byte colour format) and find the station that sets the pace. Bake the caustics to reach 25 ms, and watch the bottleneck move to memory when murk layers arrive. Then the night capture: open four kinds of GPU tool on a 31.2 ms frame, see what each can and can't tell you, and fix the caustics pass the right tool points at.

  • The four stations: vertex, raster, pixel, output & memory
  • The slowest station sets the GPU time
  • One lever per station; busy % per station
  • Fixing the limiter, then the next one in line
  • A budget per station, not only a total
  • Which GPU tool answers which question
  • Per-pass counters vs per-draw timings on tile GPUs
  • Lesson 034 challenge: predict, then check
Open lab →
liveLessons 024, 025, 027, 028simulation

Draw Call Lab

The Reef's 1,200 fish were free on the GPU, but one line, renderer.material, made 1,200 material copies: 1,550 draw calls, 1,250 switches and a 42.5 ms render thread. Share the materials (18.62 ms), try static batching (+18 MB), then instance the fish (7.88 ms). New: the Overdraw mode. The Big Catch splash paints 8.0 screens of see-through pixels and takes the GPU to 58 ms. See it as a heatmap, then cut it with cutout shapes, a size cap and a murk fade, down to 27 ms. New: the Culling mode. Lantern Harbor sends 3,120 objects nobody can see: GPU 45.2 ms. See them in red on a map, then add frustum culling for the props, occlusion for the street, and HLOD for the lighthouse view, and compare both cameras. New: the LOD mode. From the ferry, 500 houses and 3,000 pines send 3,360,000 vertices: GPU 45 ms. See the red "too many vertices for the pixels" map, then add house LODs, impostor cards for the far pines, cross-fades, and an LOD bias for the low-end phone.

  • Draw calls and material switches as CPU paperwork
  • Material copies vs shared materials + property blocks
  • Static batching and GPU instancing, and their prices
  • Overdraw heatmap: pixels, not particles
  • Cutout shapes, size caps and a fill budget in screens
  • Frustum, occlusion and HLOD culling, and their own costs
  • Checking every camera, not one
  • LOD levels, pixels per vertex and impostors
  • Cross-fades and LOD bias per phone
Open lab →

Shader Lab

The Reef's all-in-one ReefLit shader computes all 10 features on every pixel: 35 cycles instead of 20, and the GPU jumps from 27 to 36 ms. Turn the features into 12 multi_compile keywords and the GPU is fine, but 4,096 variants take 41 minutes to build. Switch to shader_feature (24 variants, 14.4 s), then fix the night glow that went missing with a uniform branch: 27.84 ms.

  • Shader cost in cycles per pixel
  • Why "× 0" is not free
  • Variant explosion: 2 to the power of keywords
  • multi_compile vs shader_feature, and missing variants
  • Uniform vs divergent branches
Open lab →

Lantern Harbor loads 720 MB of textures on the low-end phone: with the rest of the game that is 1,320 MB, and the phone kills apps at about 1,100. Turn off a forgotten Read/Write flag, compress the raw terrain and UI to ASTC, then choose between a max size and mip streaming, and watch the rod zoom fight the streaming budget.

  • Read/Write and the hidden CPU copy
  • RGBA32 vs ASTC 4×4 vs 6×6
  • Max size per platform vs mip streaming
  • Streaming budgets, soft textures and pop-in
  • Testing memory on the cheapest phone

Lighting Lab

The Lantern Festival puts 120 point lights over the market street. Forward with 4 lights per object is fast (21 ms) but misses 62% of the light.   • Per-object light limits and big meshes
  • Deferred: G-buffer bandwidth, water and CPU per light
  • Forward+ tiles and the tile-size dial
  • Baking the lights that never move

How labs grow with the course

Not every lesson needs a new lab. When a later lesson goes deeper into the same idea, it adds a new mode and new steps to an existing lab. That keeps the labs small and lets you compare old and new ideas side by side.
